intro: How the browser runs your code, schedules work and stores data.

entries.short: Parse, bytecode, interpret, then JIT-compile hot code.
entries.medium: The interpreter starts fast so the page is interactive, and the optimising compiler catches up on hot functions. If an assumption breaks, the engine deoptimises and falls back.
entries.detail: The JIT optimises by object shape. Keeping objects monomorphic, always the same properties and types, keeps property access fast.

entries.short: Objects with the same shape share a fast property layout.
entries.medium: Creating objects the same way gives them the same hidden class, turning property access into a fast offset lookup. Adding or deleting properties, or mixing types, changes the shape and can slow access.
entries.detail: Initialise all properties in the constructor and avoid deleting them to stay monomorphic.

entries.short: Generational; leaks come from references that stay reachable.
entries.medium: New objects are collected cheaply in a young generation; survivors are promoted. A leak is not forgotten memory but memory still referenced, usually by a lingering closure, an event listener or an unbounded cache.
entries.detail: Detach listeners, abort fetches and clear intervals when a component unmounts to let the collector reclaim.

entries.short: Browser, renderer, network and GPU processes.
entries.medium: Each site usually gets its own renderer process for security and stability. Inside a renderer, the main thread runs JS, style, layout and paint, while the compositor, raster threads and workers run elsewhere.
entries.detail: Process isolation is why a crash in one tab does not take down the browser, and why cross-origin iframes are restricted.

entries.short: One thread runs JS, style, layout and paint.
entries.medium: A long task there delays input and frames, which is what INP measures. The compositor can scroll and animate transform and opacity without the main thread, so those stay smooth.
entries.detail: Break up work, yield with scheduler.yield, and move heavy computation to a worker.

entries.medium: Cookies are small and sent with requests. localStorage is synchronous and string-only. sessionStorage is per tab. IndexedDB is async and suited to large structured data. The Cache API stores responses for service workers.
entries.detail: Storage can be evicted under pressure. Request persistence with navigator.storage.persist when the data matters.

entries.short: The only storage the server sees automatically.
entries.medium: About 4 KB each and sent on every matching request, so they are for small values like a session id. HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite control access and sending.
entries.detail: They add to every request, so never store data there that the server does not need.

entries.short: Cross-site cookies are blocked or partitioned.
entries.medium: SameSite=Lax is the default, Safari blocks third-party cookies, and Chrome partitions them. Embeds, SSO and analytics that relied on a shared cross-site cookie break.
entries.detail: Use the Storage Access API, postMessage, tokens or FedCM instead, and design for first-party data.

entries.short: Tasks, microtasks and a render step.
entries.medium: After each task the microtask queue drains fully, then the browser may render, then the next task runs. Rendering never happens mid-task, which is why a long task freezes the UI.
entries.detail: This is the same model as Node, with rendering inserted between tasks instead of I/O phases.

entries.short: Run a callback before the next paint.
entries.medium: Use it for visual updates so they align with the frame and are batched. It pauses when the tab is hidden, unlike setInterval.
entries.detail: Reading layout inside a rAF callback after writing can still thrash; batch reads and writes.

entries.short: Run JavaScript off the main thread.
entries.medium: A worker has no DOM access and communicates by message passing, with SharedArrayBuffer for shared memory. Service workers are a different kind: they act as a network proxy for offline and caching.
entries.detail: Offload CPU-heavy work such as parsing, image processing or encryption so the main thread stays free for input and paint.

entries.medium: Scripts are restricted to their origin for reading responses, and sites are isolated in separate processes. CORS, cookies and iframe rules all build on these two foundations.
entries.detail: Understanding the model explains why CORS is browser-enforced and why a server must still authorize every request.
